questions.problem: What is the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ with $f(x)=\frac{3x+4}{6-15x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{3x+4}{6-15x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{3x}{x}+\frac{4}{x})}{(\frac{6}{x}-\frac{15x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(3+\frac{4}{x})}{(\frac{6}{x}-15)} \\  & =\frac{3+0}{0-15} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-\frac{1}{5}.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{2}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{{x}^{3}+x}{2{x}^{2}+x+4} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(x+\frac{1}{x})}{(2+\frac{1}{x}+\frac{4}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{(x+0)}{(2+0+0)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\,\,\frac{x}{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{4}+1}{{x}^{3}-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{4}+1}{{x}^{3}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(x+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(x+0)}{(1-0)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }x \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

The limit does not come out to a finite number. Therefore, there is no horizontal asymptote.

questions.problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{9{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x}{5{x}^{2}+3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{2}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{9{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-x}{5{x}^{2}+3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{9{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{5{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(9x+1-\frac{1}{x})}{(5+\frac{3}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(9x+1-0)}{(5+0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(9x+1) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

The limit does not come out to a finite number. Therefore, there is no horizontal asymptote.
